title: Lecture 8 – Cornea
html:
Source: c8cornea.pptx – 21 slides

Cornea #1

Diseases #2

  • Mostly keratitis.
  • exogenous and endogenous
  • Exogenous inflammations
  • corneal ulcer
  • lagophthalmic keratitis
  • Endogenous inflammations
  • (1) superficial
  • (2) profound or parenchymatous
  • deeply localized

Corneal ulcer (corneal ulcer with hypopion), #3

  • in adult and elderly persons.
  • Protective Mechanisms of the Cornea:
  • Reflexive eye closing.
  • Flushing effect of tear fluid (lysozyme).
  • hydrophobic epithelium forms a diffusion barrier.
  • Epithelium can regenerate quickly and completely.

Corneal ulcer (corneal ulcer with hypopion), #4

  • Etiology. :
  • Predisposing factors that promote inflammation:
  • Blepharitis.
  • Infection of the ocular adnexa (dacryostenosis accompanied by bacterial infestation of the lacrimal sac).
  • Changes in the corneal epithelial barrier (bullous keratopathy or dry eyes).
  • Contact lenses.
  • Lagophthalmos.
  • Neuroparalytic disorders.
  • Trauma.
  • Topical and systemic immunosuppressive agents.

Corneal ulcer (corneal ulcer with hypopion), #5

  • a) preexisting chronical lacrimation due to:
  • obstruction of the naso-lacrimal duct with or without dacryocystitis
  • chronic conjunctivitis.
  • b) small ocular trauma that produces a corneal erosion;
  • changes into an ulceration after a secondary infection with pathogens (Viruses. Bacteria. Acanthamoeba. Fungi) coming from the lacrimal sac

Corneal ulcer #6

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • photophobia and lacrimation
  • ulceration in cornea center
  • the size of a pin’s head
  • enlarges by destroying the epithelium and parenchyma
  • descemetocele
  • a prominence of the Descemet membrane should the ulceration continue,

Corneal ulcer #7

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • corneal perforation with prolapse of the anterior uvea
  • congested iris miotic pupil
  • purulent exudate in anterior chamber
  • from the inflamed iris
  • panophthalmitis.
  • a suppurating inflammation of the uvea after perforation

Corneal ulcer #8

  • Management.
  • Prophylactical therapy directed to preexisting etiological factors
  • conjunctivitis and/or obstruction of naso-lacrimal duct;
  • Curative treatment
  • lubricants, antibiotics and mydriatics topically
  • antibiotics systemically.

Superficial inflammations Herpes simplex keratitis #9

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • the condition is unilateral,
  • corneal erosions
  • polycyclic contour
  • dendriform pattern;
  • resemble letters “L”,”M”, “Y”
  • geographical map
  • fir twig
  • superficial punctate keratopathy
  • disciform keratitis
  • lesions localized within the corneal parenchyma

Superficial inflammations Herpes simplex keratitis #10

  • Etiology
  • the virus is a saprophyte
  • mucosa of the nose, pharymx or within de dental decays
  • becomes virulent
  • febrile status
  • surgery upon the trigeminal nerve (Gasserian surgery)
  • Management
  • specific antiherpetic agents
  • iodiuridine , acyclovir
  • antibiotics topically
  • the eye should be kept padded until erosions persist.

Profound or parenchymatous inflammations #11

  • mainly:
  • syphilis,
  • tuberculosis
  • viruses

Syphylitic keratitiks. #12

  • in both form of syphilis
  • congenital and acquired
  • Symptoms and signs
  • congenital syphilis keratitis
  • allergic manifestation
  • between 6 and 16 years of age
  • bilateral,
  • the second eye after occurring within the first eye
  • Hutchinson’s triad.
  • keratitis
  • otosclerosiss
  • dental lesions

Syphylitic keratitiks. #13

  • Symptoms and signs
  • a) First stage (infiltration )
  • diffuse infiltration of the middle and profound layers of the corneal parenchyma;
  • b) Second stage (vasculrization )
  • begins after 2-3 weeks
  • the cornea is not totally infiltrated,
  • vascularization of the infiltrated layers;

Syphylitic keratitiks. #14

  • Symptoms and signs
  • c) Third stage (resorption)
  • clarifying the cornea
  • months or one year
  • always remaining a lot of sequelae
  • opacities and vessels with blood within the parenchyma that allow a retrospective diagnosis.
  • inflammation of the iris and ciliary body
  • variations of the intraocular pressure

Syphylitic keratitiks. #15

  • Symptoms and signs
  • acquired syphylis keratitis
  • unilateral
  • after 20 years of age,
  • 3-4 years after primary syphylitic lesion
  • Management
  • corticosteroids, lubricants and mydriatics topically
  • antisyphylitic treatment systemically

Tuberculous keratitis #16

  • unilateral
  • prolonged evolution
  • inflammatory signs are milder
  • recurrences
  • therapy
  • corticosteroids, lubricants and mydriatics
  • topically
  • treatment of the tuberculous lesions
  • systemically

Disciform keratitis #17

  • herpes simplex
  • a discoidal, well defined opacity in the corneal center
  • diminishing the corneal sensibility.
  • lasts months or years without resolution,
  • always a dense corneal opacity as a sequela
  • treatment
  • corticosteroids locally
  • radiation therapy.
  • surgery keratoplasty
  • should the opacity persist

Lagophthalmic keratitis #18

  • Lagophalmos=inability of the eyelids to close palpebral aperture.
  • Causes:
  • (1) palsy of the Vll-th ;
  • (2) cicatricial ectropion;
  • (3) severe proptosis;
  • (4) palpebral coloboma.

Lagophthalmic keratitis #19

  • Diagnostic
  • fluorescein dye epithelial lesions
  • Superficial punctate lesions initially,
  • larger epithelial defects
  • can progress corneal ulcer if superinfection occurs.
  • Management
  • etiological
  • local treatment
  • antibiotics, lubricants, astringents and antiseptics topically
  • temporary lateral or central tarsorraphy

Neuroparalytic Keratitis #20

  • Etiology:
  • palsy of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.
  • cornea’s sensitivity
  • sequela of damage to the trigeminal ganglion
  • trauma, radiation therapy of an acoustic neurinoma, or surgery.

Signs #21

  • As in lagophthalmic
  • loss of corneal sensitivity.
  • the blinking frequency drops below the level required to ensure that the cornea remains moist.
  • Symptoms:
  • free of pain,
  • foreign body sensation
  • eyelid swelling.
  • Treatment identical exposure keratitis
